Maladaptive Strategies.value: try hard not think about the trauma
keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: Several threat-focused and safety-behavior items imply hypervigilance for interpersonal or environmental danger (checking surroundings, avoiding night, choosing safe seats, scanning faces for threat), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. These items fit assault/combat-type danger contexts more than a medical trauma unless there is additional unreported trauma.

issues.item: Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark
issues.explanation: The threat and maladaptive-strategy items are internally coherent with each other, but they are poorly matched to the memory content provided. The memory items describe a fragmented, unreal, partially inaccessible trauma memory related to a medical crisis, not a recurrent expectation of attack from strangers or unsafe environments.

issues.item: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily' sits awkwardly with 'Story Feels Unreal' and 'Incomplete Picture'. Those latter items indicate disrupted, fragmented processing, whereas very easy verbal access suggests comparatively well-elaborated access. This combination is not impossible, but together with the other items it weakens coherence and is the clearest within-node inconsistency.

issues.item: Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark
issues.explanation: Avoiding going out at night is difficult to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness; it suggests an assault/public-danger context rather than a medical trauma context, especially when paired with avoidance of medical cues.

issues.item: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
issues.explanation: Safe-seat seeking implies fear of interpersonal attack or sudden external danger, which does not fit well with a trauma centered on a child's serious illness. It is also poorly linked to the other selected items, which otherwise point partly toward medical-trauma reminders.

issues.item: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
issues.explanation: Scanning faces and body language for threat similarly suggests danger from other people rather than threat related to illness, loss, or medical crisis, making the threat profile clinically incoherent with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the other two memory items, which describe a fragmented, unreal, and only partially accessible trauma memory. Those states can sometimes coexist, but this specific combination is hard to justify as the same dominant memory profile.

issues.item: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
issues.explanation: The cognitive formulation emphasizes a strong reciprocal Memory ↔ Maladaptive Strategies pattern. The selected maladaptive strategies (thought suppression and avoidance of medical/news cues) fit a poorly integrated, distressing trauma memory, but 'I can talk about what happened very easily' pulls against that formulation and weakens coherence with the other memory items.

issues.item: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
issues.explanation: For trauma related to a child's life-threatening illness, hypervigilance and irritability are plausible, but 'studying people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat' suggests interpersonal danger monitoring more typical of assault or violence trauma. It does not fit well with the medical-illness trauma context or with the rest of the profile, which is organized around medical reminders and fragmented memory rather than hostile people.

The Threat items are not well aligned with the trauma type and overall formulation. For a parent traumatized by a child's life-threatening illness, threat is more plausibly linked to medical deterioration, illness cues, or fear of recurrence. The selected threat items instead emphasize generalized external-danger/startle phenomena (hypervigilance to loud or unexpected sounds, irritability/aggressive arousal), which fit more naturally with assault/combat-type trauma and are hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. This mismatch is amplified by the Memory↔Maladaptive Strategies pattern: memory disorganization and avoidance of medical/news cues are coherent together, but the threat content does not connect plausibly to those items or to the specified trauma in a clinically tight way.

issues.item: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: For trauma involving a child's life-threatening illness, high alert to unexpected or loud sounds is hard to connect clinically unless supported by other items indicating a sudden catastrophic medical event with salient alarm noises. The rest of the profile centers on fragmented memory and medical/news avoidance, so this sound-based threat cue appears mismatched to the trauma context.

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoidance of hospitals/ambulances/physical examinations is plausible for a medical trauma, but within this formulation triggers are inactive and the profile provides no Trigger items linking external medical cues to the memory/threat pattern. The strategy therefore looks only partially integrated with the stated edge structure, especially alongside a profile otherwise dominated by memory disorganization rather than cue-driven reactivity.

issues.item: Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me
issues.explanation: Avoiding news reports about events similar to the trauma is a poor fit for the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. This item implies a broad media-based trigger pattern more typical of accidents, disasters, violence, or war-like events than a specific prolonged illness context, especially when no Triggers node items are present to contextualize it.

issues.item: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
issues.explanation: Strong physical reactivity to reminders implies identifiable trauma reminders/triggers, but the formulation specifies Triggers as inactive and the profile contains no trigger content to explain what evokes these reactions. Given the formulation, threat symptoms should not depend heavily on reminder-driven activation, so this item sits awkwardly with the node structure.

vignette:
Dr. Carlos Mendoza and the Silence

Carlos Mendoza had spent forty-two years as a pediatrician, and in all that time, he had learned to hold steadiness in the face of suffering-not to diminish it, but to contain it, to let it inform his decisions without drowning him. That capacity had served his patients well. It had not, as it turned out, served his son.

Miguel was eight years old when the fever came. Carlos remembers the thermometer reading 104.7, remembers the rash that appeared that same evening-petechial, spreading across his son's small chest like a map of somewhere Carlos did not want to go. The hospital. The spinal tap. The word meningitis, which Carlos understood in a way that most parents did not, which meant he understood exactly how little time there might be, how thin the margin between recovery and catastrophe. He remembers the isolation room, the monitors, the antibiotics running through Miguel's small IV. He remembers Miguel's eyes-fever-bright, confused, sometimes fixed on nothing at all. He remembers the night, around three in the morning, when Miguel's breathing changed and Carlos stood up from the chair where he had been sitting and knew, with the clarity of his training and his terror, that his son might die in the next hour.

Miguel did not die. After five days, the fever broke. After two weeks, he came home. After a month, he returned to school. The neurologist cleared him. There would be no permanent damage. Carlos had won the lottery.

But something in Carlos had fractured during those hours when he did not know if his son would live, and the fracture had never quite healed.

In the months that followed, Carlos found himself unable to think directly about those days. When the memory surfaced-Miguel's face in the hospital bed, the smell of the isolation room, the precise moment when he thought his son was slipping away-Carlos would push it down, would deliberately turn his attention elsewhere, would reach for his phone or a journal article or some task that demanded his full concentration. The effort was constant. He had come to understand that if he let his mind rest, even for a moment, the memory would bloom there, fragmentary and terrifying, pieces without a coherent shape. He could not describe it in sequence. He knew it had happened, but the narrative was shattered-images without connective tissue, sensations without explanation. He could not find the words even to himself.

At his practice, Carlos had begun to stay later, to see more patients, to fill every hour. His nurse, Rosa, had mentioned it gently: he was working harder than he had in years. He did not tell her why. He did not tell anyone. His ex-wife, Miguel's mother, had asked him once if he was all right, and he had said yes, automatically, the way one does.

What Carlos did not realize was how the vigilance had settled into his body. He was hyperalert in ways he could not quite name-watching the other children in his practice with an intensity that sometimes startled their parents, noting symptoms that were almost certainly nothing, his mind always running toward worst-case scenarios. When Miguel called from school-a simple thing, a forgotten permission slip-Carlos's heart would accelerate as though he were in danger. When his son seemed tired or complained of a headache, the old fear would spike, immediate and overwhelming, and Carlos would have to physically stop himself from ordering blood work, from doing all the things a panicked father might do rather than the things a reasonable physician should.

The negative emotions lived in him now-not constantly, but in waves. Fear that something would happen again. Guilt that he had not prevented it the first time, though he knew rationally that he could not have. Anger at the randomness, at the universe, at his own helplessness. And shame that he, who had spent his life teaching other parents how to stay calm, had been brought to his knees by his own child's illness.

It was this that finally brought him to seek help. At sixty-seven, Carlos had realized that he could not go on this way-could not keep his mind perpetually occupied, could not keep pushing down the memories that would not stay down. His son was healthy now, thriving, a teenager with no lasting effects. But Carlos was still in that hospital room, still holding his breath, still waiting for the other shoe to drop. He came to his first appointment hoping that someone could help him make sense of what had happened, could help him find the words and the story he could not seem to locate on his own.
